findings.quote: If $N$ would have to be zero or less, the object has left the surface.
findings.problem: False at the boundary value zero. When the force balance gives N = 0, the object still touches the surface with zero contact force and has not left it. For example, the 10 kg box of Example #4 pulled up by a rope with 98 N stays at rest on the table with N = 0. Only a negative value means it lifts off; zero means it is just about to leave. A student asked whether such a box rises would answer yes from this sentence.
findings.source: Second law with a = 0 for the stated case; OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, 6.1 and 6.3 (normal force at the point of just losing contact)

findings.quote: If the push is smaller than the maximum, static friction equals the push and the object stays at rest.
findings.problem: Stated as the general rule for static friction, but it holds only when the push is the only other force along the surface (a horizontal push on a level floor). It fails on a slope, which this lesson teaches: a block held at rest on an incline by a push up the slope has static friction equal to mg sin(theta) minus the push, not the push. It also fails for a push at an angle. The condition is not given, so a student can apply it where it gives a wrong answer. The Speed Tricks method (find the friction needed) is correct but this Core Concept sentence contradicts it in those cases.
findings.source: Checklist L27; OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, 6.2 Friction

findings.quote: and $\vec a$ is the acceleration in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
findings.problem: Acceleration, velocity and g carry the whole lesson but none gets a meaning, and no prerequisite lesson is named. The lesson never says acceleration is how fast velocity changes, and where it gives g ("where $g\approx 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$") it never says what g is, yet Example #3 asks the student to change g for another planet. The kinematics lesson teaches these, but this lesson gives no reminder or reference to it, so the reuse rule is not met.
findings.source: Checklist L25; LSG Teaching completeness (reuse needs an identified prerequisite with a short reminder or reference); writer-rules.md rule 1 added after round 1

findings.quote: Split any arrow that is not along an axis into components.
findings.problem: The lesson tells the student to split forces into components here and in Core Concept, and Example #11 depends on sine and cosine parts, but it never shows how to split a force (F cos and F sin of the angle) or what sine and cosine mean, and it does not name the scalars-and-vectors lesson that teaches them. The brief asks for force construction with components; a student meeting an angled pull cannot do the split from this lesson.
findings.source: Checklist L25; LSG Teaching completeness; brief: 'add an explicit isolated-object force construction with components' and 'Necessary prior knowledge: ... vector signs/components'

findings.quote: A surface can push but cannot pull, so $N$ is never negative.
findings.problem: This normal-force paragraph has four sentences; the limit is three. The opening dynamics paragraph, the inertial-frame paragraph, the first-law paragraph, the inertia paragraph, the ideal-rope paragraph and the Trap #1 explanation also have four sentences each.
"Cancelled" is the British spelling; American usage is "canceled". It appears again in Trap #2 ("That force is cancelled by drag and friction").
